def: A peptide hormone made by the corpus luteum and placenta that loosens pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix during pregnancy, preparing for childbirth.

A complication of monochorionic twin pregnancies in which placental vascular connections shunt blood from one twin (the donor) to the other (the recipient). The donor becomes small with oligohydramnios; the recipient develops polyhydramnios and heart strain.
A calcimimetic that activates the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, lowering PTH secretion. Used for secondary hyperparathyroidism in kidney disease and for parathyroid carcinoma.
The ribosome-driven process of building a protein from mRNA, reading codons that tRNAs match with amino acids. Proceeds through initiation, elongation and termination.
Synthesis of DNA from an RNA template by reverse transcriptase. Used by retroviruses such as HIV, and in laboratory RT-PCR.
Single-ring nitrogenous bases: cytosine, thymine and uracil. Synthesized by building the ring before attaching it to ribose; disorders include orotic aciduria.
The mRNA triplet AUG that begins translation and codes for methionine (formylmethionine in prokaryotes), setting the reading frame.
Directed movement of a cell, such as a neutrophil, along a chemical gradient toward its source. Chemoattractants include C5a, IL-8 and leukotriene B4.
An enzyme that seals nicks in the DNA backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds. Joins Okazaki fragments during replication and completes repair.
A repetitive DNA sequence (TTAGGG in humans) capping chromosome ends to protect them from degradation and shortening with each division. Extended by telomerase.
Programmed cell death, an energy-dependent, orderly process in which cells shrink and fragment without causing inflammation. Driven by caspases and regulated by BCL-2 family proteins.
A class of antibiotics, including rifampin, that inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Used for tuberculosis; cause orange body fluids and induce cytochrome P450 enzymes.
The initial, unprocessed RNA transcript made by RNA polymerase II, before capping, splicing and polyadenylation convert it to mRNA.
Small noncoding RNAs of about 22 nucleotides that bind mRNA and silence gene expression by blocking translation or promoting degradation.
A large RNA-protein complex that removes introns and joins exons in pre-mRNA. Made of snRNPs that recognize splice sites.
RNA-protein complexes (snRNPs) that make up the spliceosome and remove introns from pre-mRNA. Targeted by anti-Smith antibodies in lupus.
The hydrogen bonding of complementary nucleotides: adenine with thymine (or uracil) and guanine with cytosine. GC pairs have three bonds and are more stable than AT pairs.
Inactive enzyme precursors that are activated by cleavage, preventing damage to the cells that make them. Examples include pepsinogen, trypsinogen and clotting factors.
An inherited disorder of defective ciliary motion, often from dynein arm defects, causing chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis and infertility. Part of Kartagener syndrome with situs inversus.
A modified lysine in collagen formed by lysyl hydroxylase (needs vitamin C). Lets collagen fibrils cross-link, giving strength.
A laboratory technique to detect specific RNA sequences by separating RNA on a gel, transferring it to a membrane, and hybridizing it with a labeled DNA probe.
A technique that detects a specific protein by separating proteins on a gel, transferring them to a membrane, and probing with labeled antibodies. Used to confirm HIV infection.

Loss of the one normal allele of a gene in a cell that already carries a mutant allele, leaving only mutated copies. Underlies the second hit in tumor suppressor gene syndromes such as retinoblastoma.

Human chromosome whose 15q11-q13 region is imprinted; paternal deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome and maternal deletion causes Angelman syndrome. Also home to the fibrillin-1 gene (Marfan syndrome).
Short for reduction-oxidation: reactions in which one molecule loses electrons (oxidation) while another gains them (reduction).
An autosomal recessive long QT syndrome with congenital sensorineural deafness, from mutations in potassium channel genes (KCNQ1, KCNE1). Predisposes to torsades de pointes.
The outermost layer of a blood vessel wall, made of connective tissue that anchors the vessel and carries the vasa vasorum.
The innermost layer of a blood vessel wall, with endothelium resting on a basement membrane and sometimes an internal elastic lamina. Site where atherosclerotic plaques begin.
The ring of arteries at the base of the brain connecting the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems through the communicating arteries. Common site of berry aneurysms.
The anterior and posterior tibial arteries, branches of the popliteal artery that supply the leg and foot. The posterior tibial pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus.
The FDA's strongest drug label warning, highlighting serious risks such as death or serious injury.
Infarction of the front wall of the left ventricle, typically from left anterior descending artery occlusion. Shows ST elevation in V1-V4 and risks cardiogenic shock.

A congenital heart defect in which a single vessel arises from both ventricles instead of separate aorta and pulmonary artery, with a ventricular septal defect. Causes cyanosis and heart failure; associated with 22q11 deletion.
Alternate blood vessels that open to supply tissue when the main artery is blocked. Reduces ischemic damage in coronary and limb arteries.
A class IC antiarrhythmic that blocks sodium channels strongly, used for supraventricular arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation. Contraindicated after myocardial infarction.
Branched polysaccharides produced by bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans, important in dental plaque. Also used as plasma volume expanders.
The hard mineral outer coating of teeth, the hardest tissue in the body, made largely of hydroxyapatite. Made by ameloblasts and cannot regenerate.
A genus of gram-negative coccobacilli in the oral flora, a member of the HACEK group that causes endocarditis. A. actinomycetemcomitans is linked to periodontitis.
A genus of gram-negative rods in the HACEK group that causes culture-negative endocarditis.
A genus of gram-negative bacteria in the HACEK group, causing endocarditis and bone and joint infections in young children.
A procedure using heat from radio waves delivered through a catheter or probe to destroy abnormal tissue. Used for arrhythmia pathways and tumors.
Loss of movement of one or both vocal folds due to nerve injury, causing hoarseness or airway compromise. Common cause is recurrent laryngeal nerve damage.
Amino acids the body cannot make and must obtain from diet: PVT TIM HaLL (phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, lysine).
The region of an enzyme where substrates bind and the reaction occurs.
A Janus kinase family member (TYK2) that transmits signals from IL-12, IL-23 and type I interferon receptors. Inhibitors treat psoriasis.
A tyrosine residue with a phosphate added by tyrosine kinases. Serves as a docking site for SH2-domain proteins in growth factor signaling.
A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that preferentially dilates cerebral arteries. Used to prevent vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
An intravenous dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for acute blood pressure control in hypertensive emergencies.
Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of phenytoin, cyclosporine and calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine.
The main protein of HDL, which activates LCAT and helps remove cholesterol from tissues.
A statin that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Hydrophilic and little affected by CYP3A4.
The rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis, converting cholesterol to 7-alpha-hydroxycholesterol in the liver. Inhibited by bile acids; induced by cholestyramine.
A nitrate vasodilator (isosorbide mononitrate or dinitrate) used for angina and heart failure; releases nitric oxide to lower preload.
The extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal inspiration.
Hemoglobin carrying bound oxygen. Its dissociation curve is sigmoidal, shifting right with acidosis, CO2 and 2,3-BPG.
Hemoglobin with glucose attached nonenzymatically, forming HbA1c, which reflects average blood glucose over about 3 months.
A red cell enzyme that converts 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), which lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
A urinary antiseptic that releases formaldehyde in acidic urine. Methenamine silver is used to stain fungi such as Pneumocystis.
An atypical bacterium causing community-acquired pneumonia and bronchitis, often mild. Lacks a cell wall peptidoglycan; treated with macrolides or doxycycline.
Antibiotics with a beta-lactam ring that inhibit cell wall synthesis: penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams. Resistance occurs via beta-lactamases.
Sudden lung inflammation with leaky capillaries causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemia. Severe form is ARDS.
Lung cancer arising from bronchial epithelium. Includes small cell and non-small cell types, mostly caused by smoking.
Elevated pulmonary artery pressure of unknown or heritable cause (BMPR2 mutations), narrowing the pulmonary arteries and causing right heart failure.
Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours of a transfusion, caused by donor antibodies activating recipient neutrophils. Presents with hypoxia, fever and bilateral infiltrates.
A calculated reference weight based on sex and height, used to size ventilator tidal volumes and drug doses.
Respiratory support through a mask (CPAP or BiPAP) rather than an endotracheal tube. Used for COPD exacerbation and cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
A proto-oncogene encoding a transcription factor that drives cell proliferation. c-myc is translocated t(8;14) in Burkitt lymphoma; N-myc amplified in neuroblastoma; L-myc in small cell lung cancer.
Storage granules in endothelial cells that hold von Willebrand factor and P-selectin, released upon endothelial activation.
An antiplatelet drug that blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor; rarely used because it can cause neutropenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
An enterohemorrhagic E. coli strain producing Shiga-like toxin, causing bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome from undercooked beef. Does not ferment sorbitol.
Disease caused by E. coli, including urinary tract infection, neonatal meningitis, sepsis and diarrhea.
A mild inherited bleeding disorder from lack of clotting factor XI, causing a prolonged PTT, with bleeding after surgery or trauma. Most common in Ashkenazi Jews.
A pit viper whose venom causes local tissue damage, coagulopathy and bleeding. Treated with antivenom (Crotalidae immune Fab).
Enzymes (tPA, urokinase) that convert plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clots. Recombinant tPA treats ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction.
A high-energy glycolytic intermediate that transfers its phosphate to ADP to make ATP via pyruvate kinase. In gluconeogenesis, formed from oxaloacetate by PEP carboxykinase.
A plant-derived insecticide that blocks complex I of the electron transport chain, halting NADH oxidation and ATP production.
An inhibitor of complex III of the electron transport chain (cytochrome bc1), blocking electron flow from cytochrome b to c1.
A poison that inhibits complex IV (cytochrome oxidase) of the electron transport chain, like cyanide and carbon monoxide.
Organic compounds with a terminal carbonyl group (R-CHO), such as acetaldehyde from ethanol metabolism. Formed from alcohol oxidation and converted to acids by aldehyde dehydrogenase.
Lipids with attached sugar chains, found on the outer cell membrane and important for cell recognition. Examples include cerebrosides, gangliosides and ABO antigens.
A chemical oxidant used in periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining, which highlights glycogen and mucin in tissue.
Glycogen storage disease type VI, caused by liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Causes mild hepatomegaly and mild hypoglycemia.
A gluconeogenic enzyme converting fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate; inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Deficiency causes fasting hypoglycemia.
An endothelial surface protein that binds thrombin and activates protein C, shifting thrombin's role from clotting to anticoagulation.
Air cells between the nose and orbit, separated from the orbit by thin lamina papyracea. Infection can spread into the orbit, causing orbital cellulitis.
The wall of cartilage and bone dividing the nasal cavity in two. Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum is the usual source of nosebleeds.
Malignancies of the mouth, throat, larynx and nasal cavity, mostly squamous cell carcinoma. Risks are tobacco, alcohol and HPV.
An alkylating chemotherapy drug used in Hodgkin lymphoma (MOPP) and brain tumors. Causes disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
A localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis, producing a solitary lytic bone lesion with Langerhans cells and eosinophils, usually in children.
Accumulation of lymph (chyle) in the pleural space from thoracic duct injury or obstruction. Fluid is milky with high triglycerides.
A congenital fluid-filled cyst from abnormal budding of the foregut, usually in the mediastinum or lung and lined by respiratory epithelium.
A sedating first-generation antihistamine used as a sleep aid and, with pyridoxine, for nausea in pregnancy.
A synthetic glucocorticoid used to suppress inflammation and immunity, given intravenously in acute spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis relapses and transplant rejection.
Drugs that loosen or thin mucus to help clear it from the airways, such as guaifenesin and N-acetylcysteine (mucolytics).
A receptor for endothelin-1 on vascular smooth muscle that causes vasoconstriction. Blocked by bosentan and ambrisentan in pulmonary hypertension.
The cup-shaped structure surrounding the glomerulus that collects filtrate and passes it to the proximal tubule. Lined by parietal epithelium and podocytes.
Dry mouth from reduced saliva. Causes include Sjogren syndrome, anticholinergic drugs and radiation.
Spongy tissue at the iridocorneal angle through which aqueous humor drains into the canal of Schlemm. Impaired outflow raises eye pressure in open-angle glaucoma.
The most common kidney cancer, arising from proximal tubule cells. Presents with hematuria, flank mass and polycythemia; linked to smoking and VHL mutations.
Dense toxic metals such as lead, mercury, arsenic and cadmium that accumulate in tissue and cause organ damage. Treated with chelators.
An old analgesic metabolized to acetaminophen; chronic use caused analgesic nephropathy and papillary necrosis, plus urinary tract cancers.
Kidney disease with massive proteinuria and edema without significant inflammation, now called nephrotic syndrome.
A procedure that breaks kidney or ureteral stones into fragments, typically with shock waves, so they can be passed.
A benign kidney tumor made of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat. Strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis; may bleed spontaneously.
A fibroinflammatory disorder with swollen organs (pancreas, salivary glands, retroperitoneum) infiltrated by IgG4-positive plasma cells and storiform fibrosis. Responds to glucocorticoids.
A benign kidney tumor of oncocytes (cells rich in mitochondria), appearing mahogany brown with a central scar.
Prolapse of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall from weakened pelvic support, causing pressure and urinary symptoms.
The disulfide form (GSSG) of glutathione, produced when glutathione peroxidase neutralizes peroxides. Recycled back to reduced glutathione by glutathione reductase using NADPH.
A selenium-containing enzyme that uses reduced glutathione to convert hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides to water, protecting cells from oxidative damage.
A biotin-dependent enzyme that converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA in odd-chain fatty acid and amino acid breakdown. Deficiency causes propionic acidemia.
A 16-carbon saturated fatty acid, the main product of fatty acid synthase.
A glycolipid broken down by glucocerebrosidase. Accumulates in macrophages in Gaucher disease.

An enzyme that transfers an amino group from aspartate to alpha-ketoglutarate, found in liver, heart and muscle. Elevated AST indicates tissue damage; AST greater than ALT suggests alcoholic hepatitis.
A mitochondrial enzyme that oxidatively removes the amino group from glutamate, releasing ammonia for the urea cycle.
The enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin. Deficiency causes phenylketonuria.
A tyrosine breakdown product that accumulates when homogentisate oxidase is missing in alkaptonuria, darkening urine and causing dark cartilage.
A high-energy phosphate store in muscle that quickly regenerates ATP from ADP, buffering energy supply in short, intense exercise.
Flushing, diarrhea, wheezing and right-sided valve disease from serotonin released by carcinoid tumors, usually after liver metastasis. Diagnosed by elevated urinary 5-HIAA.
Vitamin D2, the plant-derived form, converted in the liver and kidney to active calcitriol. Used to treat vitamin D deficiency.
Irreversible scarring of the liver from chronic heavy alcohol use, with micronodular pattern and Mallory bodies. Causes portal hypertension and liver failure.
An enzyme that interconverts pyruvate and lactate while regenerating NAD+. Elevated blood levels signal tissue damage or hemolysis.
An antimuscarinic drug that relaxes the bladder detrusor muscle, treating overactive bladder. Side effects are dry mouth and constipation.
Use of drugs to suppress uterine contractions and delay preterm labor. Agents include nifedipine and terbutaline.
Drugs that mimic or block the sympathetic or parasympathetic nervous systems.
A selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor used for ADHD, a non-stimulant option.
An antiepileptic metabolized to phenobarbital, used for essential tremor and seizures.
Measurements describing red cell size and hemoglobin content: mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin and red cell distribution width. Used to classify anemias.
The most severe malaria, caused by Plasmodium falciparum. Infects red cells of all ages, causing cerebral malaria, high parasitemia and banana-shaped gametocytes.
Anemia from deletion of alpha-globin genes. Four-gene deletion causes hydrops fetalis; three-gene deletion causes hemoglobin H disease with HbH (beta tetramers).
A plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin. Low in intravascular hemolysis.
A purple dye used in Gram staining, retained by gram-positive bacteria.
An aromatic hydrocarbon solvent and carcinogen that damages bone marrow, causing aplastic anemia and acute leukemia.
Chemotherapy drugs that mimic natural nucleotide building blocks and block DNA synthesis in S phase. Examples include methotrexate, 5-FU and cytarabine.
A cytokine that stimulates marrow production of neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages. Recombinant form is sargramostim.
Poisons that damage or block nerve function, such as tetrodotoxin (blocks sodium channels) and botulinum toxin.
A mast cell stabilizer that blocks release of histamine, used to prevent asthma and allergic rhinitis. Not for acute attacks.
A mitochondrial protein involved in iron-sulfur cluster assembly. Reduced in Friedreich ataxia from GAA repeat expansion.
A foot deformity with an abnormally high arch. Associated with neuromuscular disease such as Friedreich ataxia and Charcot-Marie-Tooth.
A family of secreted signaling proteins (Sonic hedgehog) that pattern the embryo, including the midline and limbs. Mutations cause holoprosencephaly; pathway activation drives basal cell carcinoma.
A congenital hindbrain malformation with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, a large posterior fossa cyst and enlarged fourth ventricle. Causes hydrocephalus and developmental delay.
A bone marrow stem cell that gives rise to T cells, B cells and NK cells.
AML (M7) of immature platelet precursors, strongly associated with Down syndrome in children. Causes marrow fibrosis.
Abnormal sensitivity to everyday sounds. Seen with stapedius paralysis in facial nerve palsy.
The muscular back part of the roof of the mouth. Elevates to close the nasopharynx during swallowing; deviates away from a vagus nerve lesion.
A lymphoma of mature T cells, such as peripheral T-cell lymphoma and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides).
The cranial nerve IV nucleus in the midbrain tegmentum. Its axons cross and exit dorsally, innervating the contralateral superior oblique muscle.
The upper segments (C1-C8) of the spinal cord, supplying the neck, diaphragm (C3-C5) and arms. Contains the spinal accessory nucleus.
The fluid-filled spiral tube (scala media) inside the cochlea containing the organ of Corti and endolymph.
The sodium-rich fluid in the scala vestibuli and scala tympani surrounding the membranous labyrinth in the inner ear.
Hair-like projections on hair cells of the inner ear that bend with sound or head motion, opening ion channels to generate signals.
Abnormal bone growth that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, causing progressive conductive hearing loss in young adults. Often autosomal dominant.
A hole in the eardrum from infection, trauma or pressure, causing conductive hearing loss and sometimes ear drainage.
The region of the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann areas 41, 42) that processes sound. Receives bilateral input from the medial geniculate nucleus.
The space between the cerebellum and pons containing cranial nerves VII and VIII. Site of vestibular schwannoma, causing hearing loss, tinnitus and facial weakness.
A pontine nucleus that is the main source of norepinephrine in the brain. Involved in arousal, stress and panic; degenerates in Parkinson disease.
Involuntary rhythmic eye movements, with a slow drift and a fast corrective phase. Vertical forms suggest brainstem or cerebellar disease; horizontal may be vestibular.
A C-shaped nucleus of the striatum in the basal ganglia that helps regulate movement and cognition. Atrophies in Huntington disease.
Endogenous opioid peptides that bind opioid receptors, reducing pain signals in the spinal cord and brain.
The middle, pigmented layer of the eye: iris, ciliary body and choroid. Inflamed in uveitis.
Exaggerated pain from a normally painful stimulus. Allodynia is pain from a normally harmless stimulus, such as light touch.
The six-layered outer cortex, the evolutionarily newest part of the brain, responsible for perception, language and reasoning.
Brain injury from inadequate oxygen or blood flow, as with cardiac arrest or perinatal asphyxia. Neurons in the hippocampus, cerebellum Purkinje cells and watershed areas are most vulnerable.
Memory stored for extended periods, divided into explicit (declarative) and implicit (procedural). Consolidation involves the hippocampus.
Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the nose after skull base fracture or surgery. Clear fluid contains glucose and beta-2 transferrin, with meningitis risk.
Meningeal infection by fungi, such as Cryptococcus in AIDS patients or Coccidioides. Subacute course with high opening pressure; India ink shows encapsulated yeast.
The space between the dura mater and the vertebral canal wall, containing fat and veins. Site of epidural anesthesia and epidural hematomas.
Triangular excitatory neurons of the cerebral cortex and hippocampus with a long apical dendrite. Corticospinal neurons are pyramidal cells in layer V.
A neural tube defect where brain tissue protrudes through a skull opening, most often occipital.
Blinking in response to touching the cornea. Afferent limb is the trigeminal nerve (V1), efferent is the facial nerve.
Frontal lobe cognitive skills of planning, judgment, working memory and impulse control. Impaired in frontal lobe damage.
The inactive precursor of pepsin, secreted by gastric chief cells and activated by stomach acid. Pepsin digests proteins.
Mucus-secreting glands in the duodenal submucosa that release alkaline mucus to neutralize stomach acid. Hypertrophy with peptic ulcer disease.
Aggregates of bile salts and lipids, with hydrophobic cores, that carry fat digestion products to the intestinal wall for absorption.
White, corrugated patches on the sides of the tongue in immunocompromised (especially HIV) patients, caused by Epstein-Barr virus. Cannot be scraped off, unlike thrush.
The inner lining of the esophagus, made of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Replaced by columnar epithelium in Barrett esophagus.
The sphincter between the terminal ileum and cecum, controlling flow and blocking colon bacteria from entering the small bowel.
The gram-positive actinomycete causing Whipple disease, with malabsorption, arthralgia and neurologic symptoms. PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the small bowel.
Virtual colonoscopy: a CT scan of the air-filled colon used to screen for polyps and cancer.
The coordinated contractions that move food through the GI tract, controlled by the enteric nervous system and hormones.
A congenital variant where the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts fail to fuse, so most secretions drain through the smaller minor papilla. Can cause recurrent pancreatitis.
A congenital dilation of the bile duct. Presents with jaundice, abdominal mass and pain in children; raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
A venomous spider whose bite causes a necrotic skin ulcer and sometimes hemolysis from sphingomyelinase in the venom.
A cluster of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain that projects to the cortex. Degenerates in Alzheimer disease, reducing acetylcholine.
A hypothalamic region that regulates body temperature and sleep. The sexually dimorphic nucleus lies here; contains GnRH neurons.
Sleepwalking, an NREM parasomnia occurring in slow-wave sleep (stage N3), common in children.
A monophasic demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord, typically after a viral infection or vaccination in children. Causes multifocal neurologic deficits and encephalopathy.
Human chromosome involved in the Philadelphia translocation t(9;22) forming BCR-ABL, DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) and NF2.
The protein encoded by the NF1 gene, a tumor suppressor that inactivates RAS. Loss causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
Fluid accumulation in the central retina (macula), blurring central vision. Common in diabetic retinopathy and after retinal vein occlusion.
Bone marrow-derived stem cells that circulate and contribute to new blood vessel formation.
Vision from only one eye; lacks depth perception from binocular disparity.
A destructive collection of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear, behind the eardrum. Causes chronic ear discharge and conductive hearing loss, eroding bone.
Learning in which a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to trigger a response by itself, as in Pavlov's dogs.
A childhood behavior disorder with a pattern of angry mood, argumentative and vindictive behavior toward authority, without violating others' rights as in conduct disorder.
Disorders of sudden, repetitive movements or vocalizations. Tourette syndrome has multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for over a year; transient tic disorder lasts under a year.
A psychotic disorder with fixed, nonbizarre delusions for at least a month, with otherwise intact functioning and no prominent hallucinations.
Intense, persistent yearning and preoccupation with a deceased person lasting over 6-12 months after the death, causing significant impairment.
An intravenous anesthetic induction agent that causes minimal hemodynamic change but suppresses adrenal steroid synthesis.
A muscle relaxant that blocks the ryanodine receptor, stopping calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Treats malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
A combination sublingual drug (Suboxone) for opioid use disorder. Buprenorphine is a partial mu agonist; naloxone deters injection misuse.
A long-acting amide local anesthetic that blocks sodium channels. Overdose causes cardiotoxicity.
A nonselective MAO inhibitor antidepressant, used in atypical depression. Risks hypertensive crisis with tyramine and serotonin syndrome.
A personality disorder with rigid perfectionism, orderliness and control, in which the person sees the behavior as correct (ego-syntonic), unlike OCD.
A tricyclic antidepressant with strong serotonin reuptake inhibition, used for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Anxiety, intrusive memories and avoidance lasting 3 days to 1 month after a traumatic event. If longer than a month it becomes PTSD.
A serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor approved for fibromyalgia.
A growth factor released from platelets and endothelium that stimulates fibroblast and smooth muscle proliferation and wound healing.
A class of antiepileptics including phenytoin, which blocks sodium channels. Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism.
A personality disorder of detachment from relationships and restricted emotion; the person prefers solitude and is indifferent to praise, without psychosis.
The new bone and cartilage that forms around a fracture during healing, bridging the gap before remodeling.

Engorgement of the corpora cavernosa with blood, triggered by parasympathetic stimulation and nitric oxide. Nocturnal penile tumescence occurs in REM sleep and helps distinguish psychogenic from organic erectile dysfunction.
A low-potency antipsychotic that causes QT prolongation and retinal deposits.
A COMT inhibitor used with levodopa in Parkinson disease to prolong its effect. Risk of hepatotoxicity.
Toxicity from opioids causing respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils and coma. Reversed with naloxone.
Synthetic delta-9-THC used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and appetite loss in AIDS.
An organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic toxicity. Also used topically for head lice.
A cholinesterase inhibitor used for Alzheimer and Parkinson dementia.
A cholinesterase inhibitor that raises acetylcholine, used for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease. Side effects include bradycardia and nausea.
A surgical opening in the neck into the trachea to secure the airway or support long-term ventilation.
A nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker used for rapid intubation. Reversed by sugammadex.
